extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (intro / first-year) learning to write and present proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing clear, correct, and well-presented mathematical proofs (primarily for first-year undergraduates). Covers language/symbols, proof techniques (direct, cases, induction, contradiction, contrapositive), common mistakes, and basics of sets/functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics is a language — use words and symbols appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics at university is a language; use symbols as shorthand but include words and full sentences to explain steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols save time, but a proof consisting only of symbols and no words is 'nearly always' a bad proof. Lecturers advise using words (especially early on) instead of heavy notation until comfortable. Include explanations of what is happening at each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define notation and quantify carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Present commonly used symbols, Greek letters, quantifiers (∀, ∃), and set/function notation clearly so reader knows meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify domain and codomain when defining functions; do not rely on implied domains. Prefer words to introduce notation until it's standard. Misuse of quantifiers or undefined notation leads to confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and completeness — no gaps in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The final version of a proof should be clear and have no gaps; include every step needed for the reader to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not skip simple steps with 'I know what I mean' — the reader must be able to answer every ‘why?’ they might ask. Use full sentences to connect steps. If a step uses a known theorem or axiom, name or cite it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer vs reader perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs imagining an inquisitive reader who will question each step; structure the argument to preempt those questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of a proof as a 'battle' between reader and writer — ensure the argument flows and gives answers to anticipated 'why?' queries. When revising, try to fill gaps that a reader would spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical sequence: statements must imply one another
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is a sequence of logical statements, one implying another, giving explanation of why a statement is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from axioms/hypotheses or previously established theorems and deduce the conclusion by correct implications. Keep direction of implication straight (don't reverse implications unless justified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use axioms and previously proved results appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: It's legitimate and often necessary to refer to axioms or earlier theorems to justify steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very simple algebraic facts you may explicitly cite axioms (e.g., additive inverse, associativity) when appropriate, especially in axiomatic proofs. Use standard results by name when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid symbol-only proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols are useful shorthand but proofs should include words and explanations, not just a sequence of symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers (and markers) expect explanations. Use words to explain reasoning between symbolic manipulations—especially early in your studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct use of implication and iﬀ (⇐⇒) statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect direction in implications (A ⇒ B means A is sufficient for B); for 'if and only if' prove both directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove A ⇔ B, split into two parts: show A ⇒ B and B ⇒ A. Use vocabulary: 'necessary' vs 'sufficient' correctly. Beware that proving X ⇒ true does not prove X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof method
rubrics_metrics.description: For propositions A ⇒ B: start with hypothesis A, write what it means, and deduce B via valid implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include all steps; don't omit intermediate algebra or reasoning. Use rough notes or an idea sketch first, then write the tidy formal proof. Watch for tempting skips of 'obvious' steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases (exhaustion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Split the problem into finitely many exhaustive cases and prove the claim for each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a wise splitting to balance tractability and completeness. Ensure every possible case is covered — missing a case invalidates the proof. Be careful if there are many cases (higher risk of error).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (base, hypothesis, step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use induction to prove statements P(n) for all (suitable) natural numbers by checking base case(s), assuming P(k) and proving P(k+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state the induction base, the induction hypothesis, and the induction step. Conclude explicitly 'by the Principle of Mathematical Induction'. For sequences or inequalities find an explicit N when needed (e.g., limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variants of induction: strong, shifted base, multiple assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use strong induction, change the base index r, or assume several previous values (P(k), P(k−1), ... ) when required by the problem structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State which induction principle you use (standard, strong). If you assume more than one prior case, check and provide the necessary base cases (e.g., P(1) and P(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the hypothesis (if given) together with the negation of the conclusion and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain clearly what negation is being assumed and show how it leads to an explicit contradiction with axioms or known results. Note subtle differences between contradiction and contrapositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove A ⇒ B by proving ¬B ⇒ ¬A (the contrapositive), which is logically equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes contrapositive is more natural. Explain equivalence and use this technique when direct approach is awkward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of counterexamples to disprove conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: One counterexample suffices to disprove a universal conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing a statement, look for specific counterexamples. Provide a clear explanation why the counterexample violates the claim. Examples given: primes n with 2^n−1 not necessarily prime; integers not always sum of two squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spot and avoid common fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of common invalid moves: cancelling zero, assuming what you must prove, careless square roots (sign issues), reversing implications incorrectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When canceling factors, ensure they are nonzero. When taking square roots, remember ± and domain/sign issues. Avoid arguments that start from the conclusion and go to a true statement — only a forward valid chain proves the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a 'rough notes' or idea sketch before formal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Include (or at least prepare) a rough outline of the thought process to show how you arrived at the proof and to guide the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rough notes can state strategy, substitutions to try, or identities to apply; they help the reader understand motivation. Formal proof should follow the sketch in tidy steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality and case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For absolute value inequalities, splitting into sign cases for variables is standard and often needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define |x| by cases, then treat x,y sign combinations (both nonnegative, both nonpositive, one of each) and possibly subcases. Use 'without loss of generality' when symmetry permits, but still justify coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of diagrams (Venn) for sets as intuition but supply formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Venn diagrams are useful to visualise set identities, but are not formal proofs — follow with symbolic arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw separate pictures for LHS and RHS to check correctness, then write element-wise formal proof (∀x, x∈LHS ⇔ x∈RHS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theory: define operations and prove equality element-wise
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving set equalities, use 'x ∈ LHS ⇔ x ∈ RHS' and standard definitions of union, intersection, complement, subset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State definitions (x∈A∪B iff x∈A or x∈B, etc.), then manipulate logical statements. Use distributive and De Morgan laws with elementwise arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions: specify domain, codomain, and rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A function must be defined by domain, codomain, and a rule; writing f(x)=... alone is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state f : A → B and f(x)=...; equal functions must have equal domain and codomain as well as the same rule. Clarify image vs codomain (range).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image and preimage correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish image f(X) = {b ∈ B | b = f(a) for some a ∈ X} from preimage f^{-1}(Y) = {a ∈ A | f(a) ∈ Y}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct notation and explain when preimage may be empty. Warn that f^{-1}(Y) notation does not imply existence of inverse function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of functions: domain/codomain compatibility and non-commutativity
rubrics_metrics.description: To form g◦f the codomain of f must equal the domain of g; composition order matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check compatibility before composing. Example: g◦f and f◦g can give different results; show with explicit evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injective, surjective, bijective definitions and tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Use formal definitions: injective (f(a)=f(b) ⇒ a=b), surjective (image = codomain), bijective = both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove injectivity by assuming f(x1)=f(x2) and deducing x1=x2; prove surjectivity by showing every b in codomain has preimage. To get bijection sometimes restrict domain/codomain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse functions require bijectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: An inverse function f^{-1} exists only if f is bijective; composition with inverse yields identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State existence condition and demonstrate f^{-1}(f(x))=x and f(f^{-1}(y))=y. Mention domain restrictions needed to make non-bijective functions invertible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even and odd function definitions and symmetry tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Even: f(−x)=f(x) and domain closed under negation; odd: f(−x)=−f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graph symmetry to check but provide algebraic verification. Examples: x^2 even, x^3 odd. Ensure domain includes −x whenever x is included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude proofs explicitly and reference the used principle/theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Finish proofs with a clear concluding sentence which references the method/principle used (e.g., 'by induction', 'thus contradiction achieved').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A neat closing (‘Therefore …’, ‘Hence proved’, or 'by the Principle of Mathematical Induction') helps the reader see the result is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common pitfalls and 'hard parts' checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of recurring difficulties: choosing a starting point, skipping steps, not covering all cases, incorrect induction step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use checklist when writing: (1) have you defined terms? (2) did you cover all cases? (3) can any cancellation be invalid? (4) have you justified each implication? Address each 'hard part' section guidance when applicable.
